changes.after: A lazy property waits until its first read, then keeps its successful result.

before: val title by lazy { ... } declares a delegated property. Its initializer runs on the first access, then a successful result is cached. It is not rerun for every access.

The initializer reads captured state at initialization time. Later changes to that state do not replace the cached result. Default lazy initialization is synchronized on JVM, but that does not make arbitrary operations on a mutable result thread-safe; this example is sequential.

Expected output or behavior: first
first. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

after: In `val title by lazy { source }`, lazy manages the property's starting value. The block waits until code first reads title. A successful result is cached, meaning saved for later reads.
The block reads source at that first access. Later changes to source do not replace the saved title. Creating the lazy property and reading it for the first time are separate moments.
Both lines show `first`. The first read saves first as title. Changing source afterward does not change that saved result.

This example runs one instruction path at a time. The default JVM lazy setup coordinates its first initialization across threads, but that does not make all later changes to a mutable result safe to share.
